description: Add and remove Gmail labels on up to 1000 messages in one call. Pass message ids plus the label ids to add and/or remove - for example add "STARRED" or remove "UNREAD" to mark messages read. Labels are applied to every listed message together: the call either changes all of them or none of them.

message_ids.description: The messages to relabel. Gmail's own limit is 1000 per call.

add_label_ids.description: Label ids to add to every listed message, for example STARRED.

remove_label_ids.description: Label ids to remove from every listed message, for example UNREAD to mark them read.

input_schema.description: Give at least one label id to add or to remove; a call that would change nothing is refused.

response_schema.description: users.messages.batchModify has no response schema in the Gmail discovery document, which is how Google spells HTTP 204 with an empty body. There is nothing to validate on success.

quirks.real_batch: The honest batch. users.messages.batchModify takes up to 1000 ids and applies the same label change to all of them in ONE call - no fan_out, no partial success, no per-item result to report. Gmail's own limit is the node's limit.
quirks.empty_success_body: The endpoint answers 204 with an empty body on success. The current http wrapper reads every 2xx body as JSON, so that success arrives in execute.ts as an invalid_provider_response carrying status 204. Nothing else in this node can produce a 204, so the status is a safe signal. Upgrade: one guard in runtime/http_request.ts parse_response returns null for a 204, then execute.ts drops the catch.
quirks.reports_its_own_ids: Gmail names nothing back, so the node reports the ids it changed rather than inventing a response the provider never sent.
quirks.why_execute: node.json declares execute.ts rather than an http mapping for one reason: batchModify answers 204 with an empty body, which the declarative mapping cannot express yet. quirks.endpoint is the mapping it would be.
